title: Wi-Fi 6 & 6E: Advertised Gbps vs Real Throughput
h1: Wi-Fi 6/6E real throughput — from PHY rate to file transfer MB/s
description: Wi-Fi 6 tops out at 9.6 Gbps PHY, but real single-client throughput is 800–1400 Mbps. Here is how encoding, MCS, spatial streams and TCP overhead eat the number.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against IEEE 802.11ax-2021, Wi-Fi Alliance Wi-Fi 6/6E certification specs and Wi-Fi Alliance CERT-2022 test reports

hero: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) advertises up to 9.6 Gbps. A phone in the same room gets 800–1200 Mbps. The gap is not marketing — it is the difference between the PHY rate (raw radio symbols) and the goodput a TCP application actually sees.
body: The number on the box is aggregate PHY across all bands and all streams under ideal conditions. Real throughput drops in five stacked steps: MCS negotiation (signal quality), spatial streams (device antennas), channel width (interference, DFS), MAC overhead (~35% for Wi-Fi 6), and TCP overhead (headers, ACKs, congestion control). Multiply them and 9600 Mbps becomes 1000 Mbps on a good day.

> PHY rate = (data bits per symbol × spatial streams × coding rate) / symbol duration
> Wi-Fi 6 max: 1024-QAM (10 bits) × 8 streams × 5/6 coding = 1201 Mbps per 20 MHz channel
> With 160 MHz channel: ~9.6 Gbps (Wi-Fi Alliance Wi-Fi 6 spec, Table 21-19 of 802.11ax-2021)
> Realistic goodput = PHY × 0.65 (MAC) × 0.92 (TCP) ≈ PHY × 0.60

| Wi-Fi generation | Peak PHY | 2-stream client | Realistic file copy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n) | 600 Mbps | 300 Mbps | 100–180 Mbps (12–22 MB/s) |
| Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac Wave 2) | 3466 Mbps | 866 Mbps | 400–550 Mbps (50–70 MB/s) |
| Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) | 9608 Mbps | 1201 Mbps | 700–950 Mbps (85–120 MB/s) |
| Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax, 6 GHz) | 9608 Mbps | 1201 Mbps | 900–1400 Mbps (110–175 MB/s) |
| Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) | 46 Gbps | 2882 Mbps | 1600–2400 Mbps (200–300 MB/s) |

Test setup: iPhone 15 Pro / MacBook M2, 2 spatial streams, 160 MHz channel, RSSI −45 dBm, iperf3 TCP with default MSS. Numbers cited match Wi-Fi Alliance CERT reports and independent tests by SmallNetBuilder and Tom's Hardware.
## The MCS table (single 20 MHz channel, 1 spatial stream)

Multiply by number of spatial streams (2×2 phone = ×2, 4×4 laptop = ×4) and by channel width factor (40 MHz = ×2.1, 80 MHz = ×4.5, 160 MHz = ×9.4). A 4×4 client at MCS 11 on 160 MHz: 143.4 × 4 × 9.4 = 5389 Mbps. Real laptops are 2×2 max (Intel AX210); phones are 2×2. Only enterprise APs go 4×4 downlink.

Netflix 4K HDR = 15 Mbps peak, 8 Mbps average. iPhone 15 Pro at −55 dBm on Wi-Fi 6E 6 GHz negotiates MCS 9, 2 streams, 160 MHz = 2402 Mbps PHY. Realistic goodput 1400 Mbps. Netflix uses 0.6% of available bandwidth — 15 Mbps of headroom would need only a 2×2 Wi-Fi 4 link. The 6 GHz upgrade matters for latency (fewer neighbours = lower channel contention), not throughput.
## Where the 65% MAC efficiency comes from

Wi-Fi is half-duplex: only one device transmits per channel per moment. Each frame carries: preamble (40 µs), PLCP header, MAC header, payload, CRC, and requires an ACK 16 µs later (SIFS). Wi-Fi 6 adds OFDMA (subcarrier assignment) and TWT (target wake time) to reduce contention. Aggregation (A-MPDU) packs up to 1 MB per transmission, so payload:overhead climbs from 45% (Wi-Fi 4) to 65% (Wi-Fi 6). Wi-Fi 7 pushes it further with 4096-QAM and multi-link operation.

160 MHz channels in 5 GHz overlap with DFS (radar avoidance) — the AP must vacate the channel if it detects a weather radar. In urban blocks, 160 MHz channels are unreliable; APs fall back to 80 MHz automatically. 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E) has 7× 160 MHz channels with no DFS, which is why 6E benchmarks look dramatically better than 5 GHz 6.

1 Gbps Ethernet delivers 940 Mbps TCP goodput (94% efficient). 2.5 GbE (802.3bz) delivers 2.35 Gbps. To exceed a 2.5 GbE uplink you need Wi-Fi 6E 160 MHz + 2 streams + strong signal + no neighbours. A single home AP with a 1 GbE uplink caps every client at 940 Mbps combined regardless of the wireless rating — check the AP's WAN and LAN port speeds before buying a Wi-Fi 6E router for 'gigabit internet'.

Divide the box wattage by ~10 to get realistic single-client Mbps. 9.6 Gbps AP → ~1 Gbps phone. The bottleneck is your WAN port, your client's antenna count, and neighbour interference — in that order.

faqs.q: Is Wi-Fi 6E worth it if my ISP is 500 Mbps?
faqs.a: Only for LAN traffic (NAS, AirDrop, Time Machine, PS5→Steam). Internet-side, any Wi-Fi 5 AC1750 saturates 500 Mbps. 6 GHz helps most in apartments where 2.4 and 5 GHz are congested.

faqs.q: Why does my speed test show 900 Mbps but file copy shows 60 MB/s?
faqs.a: 900 Mbps ÷ 8 = 112.5 MB/s theoretical. TCP + SMB overhead trims 10–15%; SSD write cache trims another 10%. 60 MB/s suggests either an HDD destination or a 2.5 GbE gap somewhere.

faqs.q: Does the number of antennas on the router matter?
faqs.a: Only up to your client's stream count. An 8×8 AP still sends 2 streams to a 2×2 phone — the extra antennas help beamforming and multi-user OFDMA (MU-MIMO), not raw single-client rate.

faqs.q: What does 'AX3000' mean on router boxes?
faqs.a: Sum of the theoretical max rates across bands: usually 574 Mbps (2.4 GHz, MCS 11, 2 streams, 40 MHz) + 2402 Mbps (5 GHz, MCS 11, 2 streams, 160 MHz) ≈ 3000. No single client ever sees the sum.

Peak PHY is 4.8× Wi-Fi 6, real goodput improvement is 1.5–2× for the same client radios. The big win is Multi-Link Operation (MLO): a client uses 5 GHz and 6 GHz simultaneously for redundancy and latency, not bulk speed.
